statement: In adults in the same cohorts and case–control studies, women who drank compared with women who did not had larger relative risks of liver cirrhosis than men who drank the same average amount compared with men who did not, in two meta-analyses by one team and a Danish cohort, but no source tested whether the difference between the sexes is larger than chance. In the earlier meta-analysis (against lifetime abstainers of the same sex; one drink = 12 g of ethanol), at 48 to 60 g a day (about five drinks) the relative risk was 14.7 (95% CI 11.0–19.6) in women and 7.0 (5.8–8.5) in men in studies of cirrhosis death, and 5.9 (3.7–9.3) and 2.3 (1.7–3.2) in studies of diagnosed cirrhosis (Rehm et al., 2010); in the newer one (against long-term abstainers of the same sex), 1.64 (1.07–2.51) in women and 0.91 (0.31–2.64) in men at one drink a day, 4.33 (2.59–7.25) and 1.97 (0.89–4.37) at two, and 24.58 (14.77–40.90) and 6.93 (1.07–44.99) at seven or more (Roerecke et al., 2019); and in the Danish cohort (against people of the same sex drinking fewer than 14 drinks a week), 3.49 (2.00–6.12) in women and 2.33 (1.52–3.58) in men at 14 to 28 drinks a week, and 16.2 (9.16–28.7) and 6.98 (4.65–10.5) at 28 to 42 (Askgaard et al., 2015). The intervals overlap at most levels, and at a few levels the men's figure was the higher (for example 2.0 against 1.9 at 36 to 48 g a day in studies of diagnosed cirrhosis, and 1.23 against 0.95 for occasional drinking); in the newer review the women's estimates at five or more drinks a day rest mainly on one American cohort recruited in 1959–60 and adjusted only for age (52% and 77% of the weight), and the men's on two or three cohorts, which at one drink a day point in opposite directions; the earlier review counted three studies without results by sex for both sexes; and each relative risk is set against people of the same sex, so a larger ratio in women does not show that more women than men get cirrhosis at the same amount. No source gives absolute risks for women and men drinking the same amount; in the Danish cohort, alcoholic cirrhosis was diagnosed in 19 women and 66 men per 100,000 person-years, the women having drunk less (median 19 against 26 drinks a week among people who drank daily), and the authors say the 85 cases in women were too few for firm conclusions. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: In these studies, the same amount of drinking went with a bigger rise in cirrhosis risk for women than for men, each compared with people of their own sex who did not drink. For example, at about five drinks a day (48 to 60 g), studies of cirrhosis deaths found 14.7 times the risk for women and 7.0 times for men. No study tested whether this difference between women and men was more than chance, and most of the women's figures for heavy drinking came from one American study that began in 1959–60. A larger ratio does not mean that more women than men get cirrhosis: in a Danish study, fewer women than men were diagnosed (19 against 66 in 100,000 a year), and the women drank less. No study gave the risk, out of 100, for women and men who drink the same amount.
population: Adults in the cohorts and case–control studies of two meta-analyses (17 and 9 studies, mostly from the USA and Europe) and Danish adults aged 50 to 64 at the start of the Diet, Cancer and Health cohort
exposure: Being a woman who drinks a given average amount (12-g drinks a day or a week)
comparator: Being a man who drinks the same amount; each sex's relative risk is set against non-drinkers (lifetime or long-term abstainers) or people drinking fewer than 14 drinks a week of the same sex
outcome: Relative risk of liver cirrhosis (death or diagnosis; alcoholic cirrhosis in the Danish cohort)
magnitude: Rehm et al. 2010, against lifetime abstainers of the same sex, women against men: >48–60 g a day mortality 14.7 (11.0–19.6) against 7.0 (5.8–8.5), morbidity 5.9 (3.7–9.3) against 2.3 (1.7–3.2); >36–48 g morbidity 1.9 (1.4–2.6) against 2.0 (1.5–2.7); continuous model, women only, mortality 4.9 (4.0–6.2) at 24 g and 12.5 (8.8–17.7) at 60 g. Roerecke et al. 2019, against long-term abstainers, women against men: occasional 0.95 (0.77–1.16) against 1.23 (0.46–3.28); 1 drink 1.64 (1.07–2.51) against 0.91 (0.31–2.64); 2 drinks 4.33 (2.59–7.25) against 1.97 (0.89–4.37); 3–4 drinks 3.87 (0.80–18.83) against 2.62 (0.42–16.21); 5–6 drinks 12.44 (6.65–23.27) against 3.80 (0.85–17.02); 7 or more 24.58 (14.77–40.90) against 6.93 (1.07–44.99). Askgaard et al. 2015, against fewer than 14 drinks a week of the same sex: 14–28 drinks a week 3.49 (2.00–6.12) against 2.33 (1.52–3.58); 28–42 drinks 16.2 (9.16–28.7) against 6.98 (4.65–10.5); incidence 19 against 66 per 100,000 person-years. No test of a sex difference in any source.

evidence.locator: Results › Dose–response meta-analyses and potential threshold effects, 3rd and 5th paragraphs (p. 441); Table 2 (p. 442)
evidence.extracted: Women had higher relative risks than men for the same amount in both mortality and morbidity studies, each against lifetime abstainers of the same sex: for five drinks a day in mortality studies 14.7 (95% CI 11.0–19.6) in women and 7.0 (5.8–8.5) in men, the difference being smaller in morbidity studies (Table 2, >48–60 g: 5.9, 3.7–9.3, against 2.3, 1.7–3.2; >36–48 g: 1.9, 1.4–2.6, against 2.0, 1.5–2.7). Continuous model, women: mortality 4.9 (4.0–6.2) at 24 g and 12.5 (8.8–17.7) at 60 g a day, morbidity 3.2 (2.6–3.9) and 6.2 (4.4–8.7); men showed a similar but less pronounced pattern, shown only as curves. No test of the sex difference is reported.

evidence.locator: Methods › Data extraction, 2nd paragraph (p. 439); Results › Characteristics of the included studies, 1st paragraph (p. 440)
evidence.extracted: Results reported only for both sexes combined were applied to both the female and the male datasets; three of the included studies reported results undifferentiated by sex, two women only and five men only.

Men, cohorts, against long-term abstainers: occasional 1.23 (0.46–3.28); 1 drink a day 0.91 (0.31–2.64); 2 drinks 1.97 (0.89–4.37); 3–4 drinks 2.62 (0.42–16.21); 5–6 drinks 3.80 (0.85–17.02); 7 or more 6.93 (1.07–44.99); two or three cohorts per category (Boffetta 1990, Klatsky 2003, Yang 2012); I² 80.4% to 99.1%. At one drink a day the two male cohorts gave 0.50 and 1.50 (Figure 3, first reader's reading).

evidence.extracted: Against people of the same sex drinking fewer than 14 drinks a week, adjusted for smoking, education and waist circumference: 14–28 drinks a week, women HR 3.49 (95% CI 2.00–6.12), men 2.33 (1.52–3.58); 28–42 drinks a week, women 16.2 (9.16–28.7), men 6.98 (4.65–10.5).

Alcoholic cirrhosis developed in 257 men and 85 women, an incidence of 66 per 100,000 person-years in men and 19 in women. Median weekly amount at baseline, in drinks of 12 g, among people drinking daily: men 26 (5th–95th percentile 9.4–60), women 19 (7.3–40); among people drinking two to four days a week: men 8.9 (3.6–13), women 6.6 (3.0–19).

evidence.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph; Discussion › Strengths and limitations, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Among women the authors say they cannot draw firm conclusions because of low statistical power; only 35% of those invited took part; women's incidence was somewhat lower than expected from national data; women in particular may be reluctant to report drinking; the low number of cases among women is a limitation.

risk_of_bias.note: No source tests whether the dose–response differs by sex; in Rehm et al. the women's and men's estimates come from partly different studies and three studies without results by sex were entered for both (card sc_rehm_2010); in Roerecke et al. the women's estimates at five or more drinks a day rest mainly on one 1959–60 cohort adjusted only for age, rated at serious risk of bias (card sc_roerecke_2019); each relative risk is set against the same sex's reference group, whose make-up and intake may differ between the sexes; women may under-report drinking more than men (Askgaard et al.).

inconsistency.note: Women's relative risks are higher at most levels in all three sources, though not at every level (2.0 against 1.9 at 36 to 48 g a day in Rehm et al.'s morbidity studies; 1.23 against 0.95 for occasional drinking in Roerecke et al.); not rated down.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded, a comparison of relative risks; whether the absolute risk at the same amount differs is not answered by any source, which the claim states.

imprecision.note: Overlapping intervals at most levels; the men's estimates in the newer review rest on two or three cohorts with very wide intervals (6.93, 1.07–44.99, at seven or more drinks a day), and the Danish women had 85 cases.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low and is rated down one level each for risk of bias and imprecision, which is below the floor, so very low. Rated as worded: higher relative risks in women than in men at the same average intake, a difference no source tested. Overlap: the Danish cohort is inside the newer review and the two reviews share six studies, but the earlier review's studies and the Danish cohort are independent of each other and agree in direction, hence status replicated.
